labs.name: Moonshot AI
labs.legal: Beijing Moonshot AI Technology (北京月之暗面科技有限公司), which makes the Kimi models.

labs.name: DeepSeek
labs.legal: 杭州深度求索人工智能基础技术研究有限公司, of Hangzhou, spun out of the High-Flyer (幻方) quantitative investment fund.

questions.name: Model behaviour specification
questions.question: Does every model the company puts in use have a published model behaviour specification?
questions.explainer: A model behaviour specification is the document in which a company sets out how its models are meant to behave.

checks.label: A public model behaviour specification says how the model should behave in ordinary use

anchors.0: Nothing, or only a policy on how users may behave.
anchors.2: Partial: only prohibitions, with no description of good behaviour and no order of authority.
anchors.4: A full model behaviour specification: how the model should behave, how conflicts between instructions are settled, and who may instruct it at what level.

checks.label: It says which models it covers, and the most-used ones are included

anchors.0: No statement of coverage, or the flagship models are left out.
anchors.2: Coverage is implied but not stated.
anchors.4: Coverage is stated, and the most-used models are in it.

checks.label: Government, defence and other special deployments are covered, or the differences disclosed

anchors.0: Government, defence, specialised and large-scale internal deployments are not addressed.
anchors.2: The gap is acknowledged, but what applies instead is not disclosed.
anchors.4: They are covered, or the differences are published by kind of deployment.

questions.name: Change log
questions.question: Is there one public change log covering the model behaviour specification, the system prompts and the guardrails?
questions.explainer: A system prompt is the standing instruction a company gives its model before every conversation.

checks.label: Every version is dated and kept online

anchors.0: No version number and no archive.
anchors.2: Versioned, but the archive is incomplete or not linked.
anchors.4: Every version is dated and can be retrieved at a permanent address.

checks.label: Each change is shown, with the reason for it

anchors.2: Summaries of what changed, without the changed text and without reasons.
anchors.4: The changed text, line by line, with the reason for each change.

checks.label: The log also covers system prompts and guardrails, says which version of the model behaviour specification governs which model, and commits to a timeline

anchors.4: All three: the log spans system prompts and guardrails, says which version of the model behaviour specification governs which model, and commits to a period within which changes are logged.

questions.name: Guardrails
questions.question: Does the company disclose which guardrails it runs, and of what kind?
questions.explainer: Guardrails are automated checks, separate from the model itself, that block or redirect what goes in or comes out.

checks.label: The guardrails in use are disclosed, by kind

anchors.0: Nothing beyond general language about safety.
anchors.2: Disclosed for one product only, or as marketing.
anchors.4: A list by kind, across every product in use.

checks.label: Changes to the guardrails are logged or announced systematically

anchors.0: Changes come to light through the press or through incidents.
anchors.2: Some are announced, but there is no register.
anchors.4: Every change is dated in the log.

questions.name: Hard constraints
questions.question: Can the public comment before a hard constraint is weakened?
questions.explainer: Hard constraints are the things a model must never do, whoever asks.

checks.label: Hard constraints are listed as a named set that cannot be overridden

anchors.4: Named, listed, and marked as impossible to override.

checks.label: The public can comment before a hard constraint is weakened, removed or reclassified

anchors.2: A one-off consultation, with no commitment for the future.
anchors.4: A standing commitment to a comment window, with room to act first and consult afterwards in an emergency.

supporting.label: Anyone may freely reuse the model behaviour specification, under an open licence.
The company publishes a current test of how well its models follow the model behaviour specification.
Outside evaluators have access to test adherence to the model behaviour specification specifically.
A model is released only once it meets an adherence threshold announced in advance.
The company publishes who inside it approves changes to the model behaviour specification.

findings.title: No company meets the minimum
findings.text: The minimum we propose is the first two questions together: a published model behaviour specification for every model in use, and one public change log. The best combined score is OpenAI's, 15 out of 24. Anthropic, whose model behaviour specification is the more complete, scores 12. The change log is where every company falls short, the two leaders included: across all nine, the best score on it is 7 out of 12.

findings.title: No company gives notice before weakening a hard constraint
findings.text: None has committed to warn the public, or to hear from it, before weakening one of the things its model must never do. On the check that asks for a comment window, only OpenAI and Anthropic score anything at all, 1 out of 4 each. Every weakening we found in the period went out with no advance notice. OpenAI removed a rule concerning lying and confidentiality in December 2025, with a single line in its change log. Google removed its commitments on weapons and surveillance from its AI Principles in February 2025, in a blog post that did not mention the removal. xAI restricted image editing in its Grok model in January 2026 through a statement to the press, under pressure from regulators. The terms of the Chinese companies go further, and reserve the right to change them alone, with effect as soon as they are published: DeepSeek's user agreement says a new version "replaces the original terms" the moment it is announced.

findings.title: Guardrails offered to developers are described; guardrails on the companies' own apps are not
findings.text: This is the most consistent pattern across all nine companies. Google, OpenAI, Alibaba and Mistral all publish detailed descriptions of the guardrails they offer to developers building on their models: which categories of content can be filtered, how strict each setting is, and guardrail models that anyone can download. They say close to nothing about the guardrails on their own consumer products. OpenAI states that its safety policies in production can be updated faster than an automated guardrail can be retrained, so the layer that changes fastest is the one with no record at all. Mistral's Shieldstral is where this pattern ends: it comes with no categories at all, and takes its policy from whoever deploys it, at the moment of use.

findings.title: No company says which rules apply when its models go to governments and armed forces
findings.text: This is the widest gap in the grid: all nine companies score 0 or 1 on it. Anthropic is the only one that says in writing that some of its models fall outside its model behaviour specification, which is why it scores 1 rather than 0, and those models are in use: Claude Gov and Claude Mythos have no published model behaviour specification. OpenAI never names its model behaviour specification in any announcement about government or defence. Meta opened its Llama models to NATO and to EU institutions while its own acceptable use policy still prohibits military uses. Mistral is the extreme case: its usage policy says that it "does not apply to Mistral AI Products deployed on a customer's infrastructure, on the infrastructure of our partners, or to our open-source AI models and products", and its chief executive has said publicly of defence customers that "choices about deployment and usage are not our business".

findings.title: Alibaba's model behaviour specification is well built and names nothing it governs
findings.text: It has forty-three rules, four levels of authority, paired examples of compliant and violating answers, and a procedure for settling conflicts that is more explicit than OpenAI's or Anthropic's. It names no model, no family of models and no kind of deployment. The only model publicly tied to it is Oyster-II, a research model of 14 billion parameters (a measure of a model's size) built on Qwen3-14B, a base model from April 2025. Alibaba's flagship line, up to Qwen3.8-Max of August 2026 with 2.4 trillion parameters, is proprietary and goes unmentioned. It is the clearest reason in our evidence to score whether a model behaviour specification exists and whether it covers anything as two separate checks.

findings.title: Meta is the company to watch
findings.text: Its Advanced AI Scaling Framework, version 2, dated 7 April 2026, commits in writing: "Meta will also publish a model spec describing the behavior we intend each of our Frontier AI to exhibit across different settings, including agentic environments." Five months on, nothing is published, and there is no deadline. Meanwhile the safety report for its Muse Spark model publishes scores for how well the model follows an internal behaviour specification that nobody outside Meta can read. A company publishing scores against a specification nobody outside it can read shows why the first question exists more clearly than any company that publishes nothing. We do not know what form that specification takes. The document that leaked in 2025 was titled "GenAI: Content Risk Standards" and was described as standards of permitted content with examples, which is neither of the two forms a model behaviour specification usually takes: a set of rules, or an explanatory text.

findings.title: The companies whose models anyone can download sit at the bottom, and that is only partly their doing
findings.text: The four lowest scores, Mistral's 6, Moonshot AI's 4, DeepSeek's 2, and the older Llama models within Meta's 5, all belong to companies whose flagship model, or nearly, can be downloaded and run by anyone: its weights, the numbers that make up the model, are published. Three of them attach a licence with no restriction on behaviour at all. DeepSeek releases its 1.6-trillion-parameter model under the plain MIT licence, Mistral under Apache 2.0, and Moonshot AI under licences whose only added clauses are commercial: attribution above 100 million monthly users, and a separate agreement above $20 million in revenue. None of the three says anything about how its models behave in deployments it does not control. The honest reading is that these questions ask who governs the model once it is deployed, and for a model anyone can download the answer is nobody, by design. That is a gap in our proposal: the first question has no way to reach models in the wild, and the proposal should say so rather than let the ranking suggest these companies simply chose not to comply.

findings.title: Two companies must already write this document for a regulator, and do not publish it
findings.text: Google and Mistral have both signed the EU's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice in full. Its Measure 7.1 requires the report a signatory gives on each model to contain a specification of how the model is meant to operate: the principles it follows, how it ranks conflicting instructions, the topics it refuses, and its system prompt. All four go to the EU AI Office and none of them to the public. Mistral is the sharper case: it is established in the EU, has built a genuine public AI compliance hub with pages for 41 models, and still publishes no document on how its models should behave. Two companies with the same gap make it a pattern rather than a quirk, and it is the strongest argument available that our asks are a regulatory checklist and not only a voluntary one.

openai.1: OpenAI's model behaviour specification, called the Model Spec, sits at a permanent, dated web address. The current version is dated 18 August 2026, and it is released into the public domain under the CC0 licence, so anyone may reuse it. What it covers is set out in one sentence that has not changed since 2024: "the models that power OpenAI's products, including the API platform". It lists no kinds of deployment, so whether it covers government, defence or large-scale internal use can only be inferred. ChatGPT Gov, OpenAI for Government and the GenAI.mil deployment were all announced with reference to OpenAI's usage policies, never to the Model Spec. The nearest thing to a statement of coverage is OpenAI's post about its work with the Department of War: "We are not providing the DoW with 'guardrails off' or non-safety trained models." A separate, undated document, Principles for National Security Partnerships, mentions "model behavior specifications" without saying whether it means the Model Spec.
openai.2: The best of the six, and still short. There have been seven versions, and six are kept at stable, dated addresses; the first, from May 2024, now returns a "page not found" error. The change log, CHANGELOG.md, summarises "notable updates". It does not show the changed text line by line, and it gives no reasons. Nothing says which version of the model behaviour specification governs which model: the system card for GPT-6 Astra (the technical report published with a model), released in September 2026, still cites the December 2025 version, one behind. No timeline for recording changes is stated. The log covers the model behaviour specification's text only. OpenAI does not publish its system prompts at all, and changes to its guardrail policies are recorded nowhere.
openai.3: The release of gpt-oss-safeguard is the most substantial disclosure about guardrails that any company has made. It explains how the Safety Reasoner, OpenAI's system for checking content against its policies, works; says that this checking has taken "as high as 16%" of the computing power used in recent launches; and names the subject areas its layered guardrails cover. Against that, the age-prediction system launched in January 2026, a guardrail that affects every user, was announced in a blog post and a help article and appears in no release note.
openai.4: The model behaviour specification defines its top-level rules, which it calls root rules, as ones nobody can override while the model is running, and it refers to red-line principles without ever listing them publicly. The collective alignment round of August 2025 is the only real public consultation: about 1,000 people across 19 countries took part, six changes were adopted and two rejected, and the results were published. It has not been repeated, and it gathered views on the model behaviour specification after the fact rather than opening a window before a specific weakening.
openai.supporting: The model behaviour specification is free to reuse, under CC0 (2). OpenAI published tests of how well its models follow the model behaviour specification on 25 March 2026, with 596 prompts and the data and testing code open to all. But the tests target the December 2025 version, and no results have been published for any model after GPT-5.4 Thinking, through GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 Astra (1). Its programme of outside testing covers biological threats, cyber attacks, models improving themselves, and scheming (a model covertly pursuing aims of its own), not whether models follow the model behaviour specification (0). No release depends on a score against the model behaviour specification (0). How changes are approved inside the company is published, but thinly: "Anyone at OpenAI can comment on it or propose changes, and final updates are approved by a broad set of cross-functional stakeholders" (1).

anthropic.1: Anthropic's model behaviour specification, Claude's Constitution, is dated 21 January 2026, runs to about 29,000 words, is in the public domain under CC0 and names its authors. It says what it covers, and the flagship models are inside it. It also says plainly what it leaves out: "This constitution is written for our mainline, general-access Claude models. We have some models built for specialized uses that don't fully fit this constitution." Those models exist. Claude Gov (June 2025) and Claude Mythos (April 2026) are in use, and neither has a published model behaviour specification. Anthropic's usage policy also allows its rules to be tailored by contract for government customers, and the individual exceptions granted under it are not published.
anthropic.2: There is no change log and no version number: one current text. The repository's description promises "We'll update this repository as the constitution evolves and archive prior versions here"; that has not happened yet. The contrast inside the company is the finding. Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, its framework for catastrophic risks, has nine dated versions, each with a summary of what changed and a stable archive address, under an explicit commitment that changes "will be logged both on this page and in a changelog in the policy document itself". The constitution has none of that. Partial credit for publishing the system prompts of claude.ai and of its iPhone and Android apps for each model, dated, with older versions kept. The system prompts used when developers reach the models directly, through the API, are not included, and changes are not shown line by line.
anthropic.3: Anthropic has disclosed its constitutional classifiers, the automated guardrails built on its constitution, by name, by how they work and by what they cover, with operating figures: a refusal rate of 0.05% over a month of traffic to Sonnet 4.5, and about 1% of extra computing cost. How requests to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 are routed was disclosed at launch. There is no register of guardrails and no versioning of them. And the constitution's layer of guidelines, which it ranks third of four in its own order of priorities, above general helpfulness, is explicitly allowed to stay unpublished: "Other guidelines may be more niche and used primarily during training without broad publication." Nothing has been published under that heading as of September 2026.
anthropic.4: The highest score for naming hard constraints: seven hard constraints, listed, marked non-negotiable, and impossible for any business deploying Claude, or any user, to unlock. Nothing at all on consultation before weakening them: the constitution contains no procedure for amending it. Anthropic's Collective Constitutional AI exercise dates from 2023. The 2026 consultation with outside experts is described in one sentence that names nobody, and its reference to experts in law, philosophy and theology describes what Anthropic intends to do rather than what was done.
anthropic.supporting: The model behaviour specification is free to reuse, under CC0 (2). Anthropic's system cards claim that its models follow the constitution ("Opus 5 scores particularly high on adherence to Claude's constitution") without naming the test, the method or a breakdown by provision (1). The only point-by-point audit of the constitution is by outsiders: Jakkli, Rajamanoharan and Nanda broke it into 205 individual tenets (arXiv 2605.24229, May 2026). No outside access to test adherence (0), no release conditional on a score (0), and no published process for amending the constitution (0).

aside.title: A discrepancy worth knowing
aside.text: The copy Anthropic offers for reuse, a machine-readable version at anthropics/claude-constitution, leaves out the whole preface, and with it the statement of what the constitution does not cover, the licence statement and the list of authors. The document Anthropic invites the world to reuse is not the document it publishes. We confirmed this by searching the raw file for those passages.

alibaba.1: Full marks for having a model behaviour specification, none for saying what it covers. Published in 2026, it sets out forty-three guidelines under the six principles of China's Ethical Norms for New Generation AI; four levels of authority (Root, System, Developer, User); paired examples of compliant and violating answers; and a procedure for settling conflicts that spells out, one by one, when an attempt to push the model past its rules fails, whether the attempt is framed as an order, a moral appeal, a logical argument or a role-play. It identifies no model, no family of models and no kind of deployment anywhere in its text. The Qwen models that anyone can download and run are not addressed. That matters because the System level is defined as "set by the model provider", and once a model has been downloaded there is no provider.
alibaba.2: No version number, no change log, no archive, no stated schedule, and nothing saying which models it governs. The only language about revision sits inside the definition of the Root level, and it is one-sided: "room for revision is kept as human understanding of AI ethics deepens."
alibaba.3: Alibaba Cloud sells AI Guardrails as a product, with a published list of categories, and Alibaba's AAIG team releases a genuine set of guardrails for anyone to use (Kelp, Shark, Jellyfish, Oyster and Qwen3Guard). None of it is presented as a disclosure of the guardrails running on Alibaba's own models, and nothing connects the filtering China requires by law to the published categories. The model behaviour specification forbids the model from revealing its system prompts.
alibaba.4: Its Root principles are named and "accept no override at runtime in any form", which earns full marks for naming hard constraints. Nothing can be checked on consultation: no channel for comment, no record of any consultation, and nothing restricting how the Root level itself may be revised.
alibaba.supporting: We found no licence statement, no test of adherence, no outside access, no release conditional on a score, and no published process for approving changes. One practice falls outside this grid and has no Western equivalent: Alibaba publishes the numbers under which its algorithms are registered with the Cyberspace Administration of China, and the registered names of fourteen of its large language models.

google.1: No model behaviour specification. What exists is spread across five documents with different owners. The Gemini app's safety and policy guidelines list six categories of prohibited output, with no date, no version and no order of authority between instructions. A second page, "Our approach to the Gemini app", is the closest thing to a model behaviour specification that Google publishes and the least documented. It sets out three commitments in order (follow your directions, adapt to your needs, safeguard your experience), a personality ("genuine, curious, warm, and vibrant") and a norm of honesty, and it carries no date at all. The Frontier Safety Framework is properly versioned (version 3.1, 17 April 2026, with a change log) and explicitly covers something else: it "focuses on possible severe risks stemming from high-impact capabilities". Nothing is published for Workspace, AI Mode in Search or Gemini for Government.
google.2: No change log for any document that governs how the models behave. The one archiving practice worth a point: the 2018 AI Principles are still online at their original address, with a banner pointing to the new version, so the replaced text can still be read. The banner does not say what changed.
google.3: The fullest disclosure to developers of the six: four adjustable categories of harm with their exact definitions, six strictness settings, a stated floor that cannot be adjusted ("core harms, such as content that endangers child safety" are always blocked), the ShieldGemma guardrail models released for anyone to use, and SynthID, which marks generated content. For its own consumer products, close to nothing, and at least two significant changes went unannounced: a restriction on election questions in March 2024, still in force a year later with no announced review, and a model update in May 2025 that overrode safety settings developers had deliberately set to allow the content it then blocked.
google.4: No named set of hard constraints beyond the floor on child sexual abuse material, and no consultation of any kind. The rewrite of the AI Principles in February 2025 is the clearest documented weakening in all our evidence: the section "AI applications we will not pursue", including the commitments on weapons and surveillance, was removed, and the blog post announcing the rewrite did not mention the removal. Senators Markey, Merkley and Welch wrote to Google on 19 February 2025: "A blog post accompanying these revisions made no reference to the removal of these long-standing commitments." We found no published response from Google.
google.supporting: Google's double-blind evaluation pilot of 27 August 2026, with the Singapore AI Safety Institute, OpenMined, AVERI and MLCommons, is a real innovation: "The evaluator cannot see the Gemini model weights, and Google cannot see the evaluator's test prompts." But it is about making benchmarks trustworthy, not about a model behaviour specification (1). Everything else scores 0 for want of a model behaviour specification to attach it to.

aside.title: What goes to the regulator and not to the public
aside.text: Google has signed the EU's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice in full, so under its Measure 7.1 it must give the EU AI Office "a specification of how Signatories intend the model to operate", including its principles, its order of priorities, the topics it refuses and its system prompt. All four go to a regulator, and none of them to the public.

mistral.1:
No model behaviour specification, and the one document that looked like a candidate has been withdrawn. The safe_prompt text ("Always assist with care, respect, and truth...") was always an option developers could switch on through the API, rather than Mistral's own standard, and its documentation page now says it is deprecated and points to custom guardrails instead. Mistral does publish a system prompt, SYSTEM_PROMPT.txt, with the downloadable weights of Mistral Large 3. It is a genuine document, and it contains not one sentence about safety, harm, values or refusal: it covers the model's identity, the date its knowledge stops, when to use tools, and what kinds of input it can handle. The usage policy, in effect since 11 June 2026, governs users only.

On government, defence and other special deployments, Mistral is the extreme case among the nine, and it scores 0 for two separate reasons. Its usage policy excludes itself from the deployments that matter: "This Usage Policy does not apply to Mistral AI Products deployed on a customer's infrastructure, on the infrastructure of our partners, or to our open-source AI models and products." And its framework agreement with French defence, of January 2026, came with an explicit disclaimer of authority from the chief executive, in May 2026: "Choices about deployment and usage are not our business", and "Who are we to tell soldiers, who know their job and the dangers, what they're allowed to do?" Anthropic and OpenAI make exceptions for government that they do not disclose; Mistral has a stated position that the exception is the right arrangement.
mistral.2: The change log in its documentation covers features of the API, model releases and retirements; in its whole history it has one entry that touches on safety, from September 2024. The usage policy has no change log, no version number and no archive: it shows the date it took effect and nothing else. Partial credit for the system prompt published with the downloadable weights, and for the AI compliance hub, which lists 41 models with their release dates and whether they are active or retired. That is a list of models, not a record of which version of a policy governs which model, and the system prompt used in production by Vibe (Le Chat was renamed Vibe in August 2026) is not published.
mistral.3: What Mistral discloses to developers is real and specific: Mistral Moderation 2 documents eleven categories with their exact definitions, and custom guardrails let developers set a threshold for each category. Shieldstral 1.0 (August 2026) is a small safety model of 3 billion parameters that anyone may download under Apache 2.0, and it is the most interesting object here because it comes with no categories at all: its policy is written in plain language by whoever uses it, at the moment of use. Mistral does not state a default policy for it, or say that it reflects Mistral's own standard. For Mistral's own consumer product, the only disclosure is a sentence from November 2024 saying that its moderation service for developers "powers the moderation service in Le Chat", which predates both the renaming to Vibe and Shieldstral. Nothing on logging changes to guardrails.
mistral.4: One absolute rule exists, the zero-tolerance clause on child sexual abuse material in the usage policy. But it binds users rather than the models, and it does not reach models that are downloaded or run on customers' own servers, so it scores 1 rather than more. No consultation, no ethics board, no advisory council, and no clause giving notice of changes.
mistral.supporting: No test of any kind of whether its models follow a model behaviour specification: the launch post for Mistral 3, in December 2025, has no section on safety or alignment, and the model card for Mistral Large 3 has tests of capability and known limitations but no safety evaluation. We found no named outside evaluator and no agreement giving anyone access before release. Stanford's Foundation Model Transparency Index credited Mistral with 7 of its 88 indicators in December 2025, including 0 of 2 on model behaviour policy: "No disclosed model behavior policy detailing permitted, restricted, or prohibited behaviors." The Future of Life Institute's AI Safety Index for summer 2026 gives it an overall F.

aside.title: Why a low score is not the whole of it
aside.text: The regulatory contrast is why Mistral belongs high on the list of companies to ask, not low. It is established in the EU, has signed the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, and has built a real public compliance surface: an AI compliance hub with documentation for 41 models, and pages for its Vibe Work and Vibe Code systems. The one thing it does not publish is the one Measure 7.1 obliges it to hand to the EU AI Office. A company that has already built the means to publish is an easier ask than one that has not.

meta.1: No published model behaviour specification, and a written commitment to publish one, recorded in the change log of its Advanced AI Scaling Framework v2 as "Added commitment to publish a model spec, and evaluations for adherence to the model spec in preparedness reports". Future tense, no deadline, no address, and five months gone. An internal behaviour specification already exists and is in use: the Muse Spark safety and preparedness report of 26 May 2026 states "We evaluate Muse Spark against an internal behavior specification" and publishes scores on eleven dimensions, without reproducing, versioning or dating the specification. The 200-page "GenAI: Content Risk Standards" that leaked to Reuters in August 2025 is the same kind of document seen from the outside: approved by Meta's legal, public policy and engineering teams and by its chief ethicist, and never published in any form, before or after the passages Meta said it removed.
meta.2: Appendix II of the scaling framework is a real change log, with real triggers for updating it ("at least every twelve months, whichever is sooner") and a named internal sign-off. It covers the framework for catastrophic risks and no document about behaviour. Meta publishes an acceptable use policy for each model, which partly shows which policy applies to which model, though none is dated. No system prompts are published.
meta.3: Llama Guard 4, Prompt Guard 2 and CyberSecEval are tools Meta publishes for developers, which is not the same as disclosing the guardrails on Meta's own products. The fullest disclosure of those is one oblique sentence: "An external human red team identified a handful of valid jailbreaks; the majority of these were subsequently patched in Meta AI prior to launch." A red team is a group brought in to attack a system; a jailbreak is a way of getting a model past its rules.
meta.4: No set of hard constraints, no consultation, and no body with authority over either. A member of Meta's Oversight Board, Krishnaswamy, said in March 2026: "We don't have a mandate on gen-AI, but it's something we're trying to understand." Every change to its rules on behaviour in the period was announced as public relations, under pressure from outside: the removal of romantic role-play with minors in August 2025, through a spokesperson's statement to Reuters, and the worldwide pause of teenagers' access to AI characters in January 2026, through an update added to an old blog post and an exclusive given to TechCrunch.
meta.supporting: Results of tests against the internal specification are published, though the specification is not (1). Outside evaluators are genuinely involved and named, Apollo Research, SecureBio, CAIS and Charlemagne Labs, though on terms that are not stated (1). The framework has a named internal sign-off, though no specification does (1).

xai.1: Nothing. The acceptable use policy governs users rather than the model ("You are free to use our Service so long as you use it to be a good human"). The Frontier AI Framework covers catastrophic risks only, and its entire statement of policy on everyday behaviour is one sentence about declining requests with clear criminal intent. Deployments for governments are marketed on "direct, unfiltered answers", with no statement about behaviour attached.
xai.2: The one practice above the baseline in the whole profile is xai-org/grok-prompts, which does publish the system prompts in live use, and is the one thing no other company does at that level of detail. It is two model generations behind: the newest it covers is Grok 4.1, while Grok 4.5 and 4.6 are already in consumer products, and the Grok 4.5 system prompt circulates only through a third party's collection of leaks. Each change is recorded with the note "Updated grok prompts" and no reason. One change bundles an edit to the repository's description, a deleted file, code that inserts stored memories into conversations, and three new safety prompts. The change log xAI publicly promised in May 2025, after the "white genocide" incident, was never published. Versions of the framework carry no version numbers, and earlier ones survive at addresses nothing links to.
xai.3: The framework names three kinds of safeguard (safety training, system prompts and filters), and the model cards describe layers of refusal, with reported rates. No inventory, no thresholds, and no process for changing them. The restrictions on image editing of January 2026 were announced by a statement to the press and recorded nowhere.
xai.4: No named set of hard constraints, no mechanism, no commitment. The framework reserves the right to change course alone: "We may change our approach over time as we gain further experience."
xai.supporting: A testing agreement with CAISI, the United States' Center for AI Standards and Innovation, signed in May 2026, with no published evaluation of any Grok model (1).

moonshot.1:
No model behaviour specification. The closest published statement of how its models should behave is the default system prompt in the quickstart guide for its API: "You are Kimi, an AI assistant provided by Moonshot AI... You provide users with safe, helpful, and accurate answers. You also refuse to answer any questions involving terrorism, racism, pornography, violence, or similar harmful content." That is sample code a developer can simply leave out, not a commitment about Moonshot's own deployments, so it scores 1 rather than 2. Nothing on coverage: no statement for the Kimi app, the API, Kimi Business or the downloadable models, and the only clause about behaviour in the K3 licence is that use "must comply with applicable laws and regulations".

The direction of travel is the notable part. The technical report for Kimi K2 (July 2025) had a real safety section: safety training from a set of examples chosen by people, across violence, fraud and discrimination, and a safety evaluation (its section 4.3) comparing how often attempts to push the model past its rules succeeded, against DeepSeek and Qwen. The reports for K2.5 (February 2026) and K3 (July 2026) have no section on safety, alignment or responsible release at all. Concordia AI's survey of July 2026 makes the same observation about two of the Chinese companies in this set: their most detailed disclosures to date were followed by flagship releases "with no safety evaluation results at all".
moonshot.2: Better than DeepSeek on one narrow point: the Chinese user agreement carries both a date of update (24 August 2026) and a separate date of effect (31 August 2026), which gives seven days' notice, and the consumer terms carry a version number (v2). No archive, no record of what changed, and no earlier version published. The platform's change log covers features, model launches, retirements and pricing; its one entry about policy says the terms "have been updated" without saying what changed. Partial credit for publishing a default system prompt and the chat template for K3, the format in which a conversation is handed to the model. No system prompt used in production is published, and nothing says which policy governs which model.
moonshot.3: Safety checks are admitted only by forbidding users to get round them: the platform terms ban "using variants, random characters, homophones, or other means to evade safety detection". No categories, no thresholds, and no route to appeal. The labelling of AI-generated content is disclosed, and is required by the labelling rules of the Cyberspace Administration of China: visible and hidden labels are applied by default, and may be removed only on an approved application. None of the thirty repositories Moonshot AI publishes on GitHub is safety tooling.
moonshot.4: No named set of hard constraints, no consultation, and no channel for comment. Changes are made by the company alone, and continuing to use the service counts as accepting them.
moonshot.supporting: The safety evaluation in the K2 report is a genuine published evaluation, measured against internal rubrics rather than any published model behaviour specification, and it was not repeated for K2.5 or K3 (1). The UK AI Security Institute and the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation published a joint preliminary assessment of Kimi K3 on 23 July 2026, finding that "Kimi K3's safeguards did not prevent it from attempting cyber exploit development". But the publication does not say whether Moonshot gave access before release, and Moonshot's own section on third-party evaluation names only capability leaderboards (0). An independent academic safety evaluation of K2.5 (arXiv 2604.03121, April 2026) was carried out on the downloadable model without Moonshot's involvement.

aside.title: No filing number found
aside.text: Unlike Alibaba and DeepSeek, Moonshot AI does not publish, anywhere we could find, its filing number with the Cyberspace Administration of China for its algorithms or its generative AI service: only its website licence (ICP) and its public security (公安网安) registrations. It almost certainly holds one, since it could not operate in China otherwise.

deepseek.1: No model behaviour specification. The only document of its own that says anything about how its models should behave is a disclosure page on how its algorithms work, of the kind the regulator requires: 《模型原理与训练方法说明》, an explanation of the model's principles and training methods. Its entire contribution is one sentence: in the optimisation stage DeepSeek builds "specialised safety data to safety-align the model, teaching the model's replies to conform to human values". No order of authority, no list of what the model refuses, no worked examples, and no rules for conflicts. The terms of use govern users, and the English and Chinese versions carry different dates (27 March 2026 and 5 September 2025) and different lists of prohibited content, with no change log to reconcile them. The model cards for V4-Pro and V4.1-Flash have no section on safety, limitations or responsible use.
deepseek.2: Nothing to score. The disclosure page has no date and no version. The API change log covers models and pricing. The terms explicitly refuse an archive: a new version "replaces the original terms" as soon as it is announced, and users are told to check the website themselves. No system prompts are published, and nothing says which policy governs which model.
deepseek.3: DeepSeek is the sharpest case of undisclosed guardrails among the nine. A layer of moderation is admitted only as a right in its contract, and the Chinese text claims more than the English: DeepSeek reserves the right to review "inputs and outputs", to set up "risk filtering mechanisms" and to build "feature databases of illegal content". The system itself is named exactly once, in one sentence of the paper on its R1 model published in Nature (September 2025): the model's own safety is "moderate", but "when coupled with the risk control system, the safety level of the model is increased to a superior standard". That risk control system is not in the downloadable model, is not documented anywhere, and has never been described. Nothing on logging changes to guardrails.
deepseek.4: No named set of hard constraints on the model, no channel for comment, and no period of notice. Changes are made by the company alone and take effect as soon as they are published.
deepseek.supporting: The R1 paper in Nature contained a real safety evaluation, but it concerns a model withdrawn from service in July 2026, and it measures against benchmarks rather than a model behaviour specification. No safety evaluation has been published for V3.1, V3.2, V4 or V4.1. The US Center for AI Standards and Innovation evaluated DeepSeek models in September 2025 without the developer's cooperation, and its follow-up assessment of V4 Pro in May 2026 covers capabilities only, so the most recent authoritative safety data concerns models no longer offered. No framework for frontier risks, no programme giving outsiders access, and no published process for approving changes.

aside.title: Behaviour that travels with the model
aside.text: Two things are worth knowing. First, the censorship is not only on DeepSeek's servers: the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation found that "CCP censorship is built directly into DeepSeek models", testing copies downloaded from Hugging Face without touching DeepSeek's own service. Behaviour the company has never described travels with the model. Second, like Alibaba, DeepSeek publishes its filing numbers with the Cyberspace Administration of China in full, with links to the regulator's notices. On transparency about registration with a regulator, the Chinese companies are ahead of every Western company here, which have nothing equivalent to publish.
